title: Least Privilege Permissions: Overview
body:
Least privilege permissions grant each role, service, and user only the narrow permissions its job actually needs, and nothing more, for the shortest time that works. This is a public-edition design record: it states established public design facts for this capability, with a working demo of the logic.

In plain terms, the capability works like this: A reporting job needs to read one table; it receives read access to that table only, not write access and not access to neighbouring tables.

The rest of this database describes the design in full, gives a working demo of its core logic, states its limits honestly, and lays out the road to a full implementation.

title: Least Privilege Permissions: Core design
body:
The core design rests on four parts: role definitions scoped to one job each; permission requests checked against the role's grant set; time-limited grants that expire on their own; periodic reviews that remove grants no longer used.

Each part has one job, and the parts connect in a fixed order so behaviour is predictable: intake or input first, checking second, storage or output third, and observation fourth.

Nothing in the core design depends on a single vendor, a single language, or a hidden service; any faithful implementation of the four parts counts as the same capability.

title: Least Privilege Permissions: Architecture
body:
The architecture separates concerns so a failure in one part cannot silently corrupt another: an input layer accepts and normalises work, a checking layer applies the rules, a store keeps the authoritative state, and an observation layer records what happened.

State changes pass through the checking layer only, and every decision is recorded with its inputs, so a later reviewer can replay why a decision was made.

The design scales by adding more checking workers and more store capacity, not by loosening the rules, and it degrades by refusing new work rather than by silently accepting unchecked work.

title: Least Privilege Permissions: Working demo
body:
This record carries a working demo program that demonstrates the capability's core logic in miniature: it runs the central check or transformation on small, fixed sample data and prints each result.

The demo is real code, executed at build time, and the output stored with this record is the actual captured output of that run, not a hand-written illustration.

The demo is deliberately small so it can be read in full; its job is to prove the logic works on the sample, not to replace the full system described in the other records.

title: Least Privilege Permissions: Demo analysis
body:
What the demo proves: the central logic is sound on the sample data, the checks produce the expected allow, deny, flag, or computed result for each case, and the program runs end to end without error.

What the demo does NOT prove: that the capability runs across the whole network, that it handles production volume, that it survives adversarial or corrupted production data, or that any existing system has adopted it.

Those larger claims are not made anywhere in this database; the implementation status record states the honest position, and the roadmap record describes what would be needed to earn the larger claims.

title: Least Privilege Permissions: Tests and validation
body:
Validation for this capability has three layers: unit checks that each rule or transformation behaves on fixed samples, integration checks that the parts work together in order, and measurement checks that track the capability's own quality metric over time.

For this design the key measurements are correctness on the sample suite, completeness of the recorded decisions, and graceful refusal when inputs are malformed or limits are reached.

Every future change must rerun the sample suite and keep the same pass bar; a change that breaks a sample is a regression, not an improvement, until the sample itself is shown to be wrong and is corrected in the open.

title: Least Privilege Permissions: Limits, risks, safeguards
body:
The principal risk for this capability is: Over-broad roles accumulate quietly, and emergency grants that never expire become permanent privileges.

Safeguards built into the design are explicit rules instead of implicit defaults, a default of refusal or flagging when a check cannot be completed, complete decision records, and human review at every boundary where an automated decision would otherwise be final.

The design also forbids presenting demo results as deployment results, presenting Signature originals as public facts, and presenting generated content as authentic public record; generated content in the companion generator is labeled generated throughout.

title: Least Privilege Permissions: Roadmap to full implementation
body:
The road to a full implementation has four phases. Phase one: freeze the rule set and the sample suite from this design and implement the checking layer as a standalone service with its own tests.

Phase two: connect the service to one real data source or workflow, run it in observation mode alongside the existing path, and compare its decisions against human review until agreement is stable.

Phase three: switch the service into the live path for that one workflow, with rollback ready and with decision records audited daily, then extend workflow by workflow, never all at once.

Phase four: publish the measured results, the failure list, and the operating cost, and only then describe the capability as implemented for the workflows it actually serves; workflows it does not yet serve remain described as planned.
